samples.summary: Design doc names the wrong cookie for the CLI login binding
samples.evidence: docs/design/cli.md:184-187 says the CLI start "sets/echoes the `wafflebase_cli_confirm` pair and the backend sets a short-lived `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie on that browser". The code deliberately does NOT use the browser flow's cookie for the CLI binding: `github-auth.guard.ts:294` issues `CLI_STATE_COOKIE` (`wafflebase_cli_state`), and the whole point of the separate name (guard doc-comment, and `docs/design/backend.md:121-123`, which gets it right) is that the two flows must not overwrite each other. The top-level design doc now documents the exact behaviour the change removed, so a future reader reconciling the two docs will re-introduce the collision.

samples.summary: `consumeCode`'s "unchallenged code" compatibility branch is unreachable now that the guard requires `code_challenge`
samples.evidence: `CliAuthStore.consumeCode` (packages/backend/src/auth/cli-auth.store.ts:120-140) and its doc-comment promise that "a code minted without a challenge (a CLI predating PKCE) stays redeemable with the code alone", and `CliExchangeDto.codeVerifier` is `@IsOptional()` for the same reason. But the only production caller of `createCode` is `auth.controller.ts:235`, which always passes `cliState.codeChallenge`, and `github-auth.guard.ts:272-274` now 400s any `mode=cli` start that omits `code_challenge`. So no unchallenged code can exist in production; the branch (and the DTO's optionality) is exercised only by tests and documents a compatibility path that no longer exists. Either drop it or note it is test-only — as written it invites a caller to assume unchallenged codes are still supported.

samples.summary: Two concurrent browser logins in one browser now collide on the single `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie
samples.evidence: The guard gave the CLI flow its own cookie name precisely because "the second start overwrites the first's binding and the first callback is refused as a forgery" (github-auth.guard.ts:24-36). The same collision still exists web-vs-web: every `GET /auth/github` without `mode=cli` overwrites `OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE` (github-auth.guard.ts:302). The frontend login link (packages/frontend/src/components/login-form.tsx:53) is an ordinary `<Link>` a user can open in two tabs, or open, go back, and open again; the stale tab's callback then fails `verifyCallbackState` and lands on `/login?error=login_state` for a login that previously would have completed. Before this change the browser callback required no cookie at all, so this failure mode is new for that out-of-diff entry point.

samples.summary: User-facing CLI docs still describe the old login flow (no consent page, no headless URL file, old timeout)
samples.evidence: packages/documentation/developers/cli.md:19-31 still says only "The CLI opens your browser for GitHub authentication". The change adds a mandatory server-rendered consent interstitial that must be clicked, a five-minute window, and — when stderr is not a TTY — writes the login URL to `<config-dir>/login-url.txt` and prints only the path (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:200-240). None of that appears in the shipped user documentation (only `docs/design/cli.md`, which end users do not read), so headless/CI users following these docs will see a message referring to a file the docs never mention. `packages/backend/README.md:389-399` likewise still documents the auth flow with no `state` validation step.

samples.summary: `isAuthPath` blanket-redacts query strings for non-credential `/auth/*` routes
samples.evidence: `isAuthPath` matches `/^\/auth(?:\/|$)/` and drops the whole query string, which also covers `UserDocStylesController` at `packages/backend/src/user-doc-styles/user-doc-styles.controller.ts:7` (`@Controller('auth/me/doc-styles')`) and any future `/auth/*` route that takes ordinary filtering parameters. Those requests' logs lose all query detail even though they carry no login material. Low impact (readability only), but it is a route outside the diff that the new rule silently changes.

finding.summary: The CLI's 30-second callback timeout was not revisited even though the backend now inserts a mandatory human consent interstitial into the CLI login flow
finding.evidence: `startCallbackServer` still rejects with `Login timed out` after `30_000` ms (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:451 — code the diff did not touch). The backend side of this change (packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:226 → `req.__cliConsent`, rendered by `AuthController.renderCliConsent`) now stops a `mode=cli` start *before* GitHub and requires the person to read an interstitial and click "Continue sign-in", on top of GitHub's own consent screen. The whole human sequence — browser launch, read interstitial, click, GitHub authorize — must now complete inside 30 s or the CLI aborts and the code never arrives. The server's own budget for the same human step is 5 minutes (`STATE_COOKIE_MAX_AGE_MS`, github-auth.guard.ts, and the 5-min `CliAuthStore` state TTL), so the two ends now disagree by an order of magnitude. docs/design/cli.md:205 and :282 still document the 30-second timeout as the flow's budget, i.e. the doc was updated for the new interstitial but the timeout was left as-is. Fix belongs on the CLI timeout (raise it toward the server's 5-minute state TTL).

verdict.reason: The finding's core evidence is absent. `packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:323` already defines `CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000`, and the only timeout in the login callback server (`login.ts:455-470`, which emits 'Login timed out') uses that constant — there is no `30_000` literal anywhere in packages/cli (only an unrelated Vitest per-test timeout at packages/cli/test/docs-export.test.ts:184). The comment at login.ts:306-322 documents the raise precisely because of the new consent interstitial, aligning with the server budget `STATE_COOKIE_MAX_AGE_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000` at packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:49. The docs cited as still saying 30 seconds actually say the opposite: docs/design/cli.md:205-206 states "a five-minute timeout". A test pins the agreement at packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:116-134. So the two ends do not disagree; the claimed defect does not exist in this repository.

finding.summary: Both login flows write the same single `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie, so a second login start in the same browser silently invalidates the first
finding.evidence: `issueLoginCookie(context, OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE)` is called for the CLI branch (github-auth.guard.ts:241) and for the browser branch (github-auth.guard.ts:250) with one fixed name and `path: '/'`. Any second start overwrites the first browser's half, and `AuthController.takeStateCookie` (auth.controller.ts, `res.clearCookie` on read) makes it single-use. Reachable out-of-diff entry point: the frontend's plain sign-in link at packages/frontend/src/components/login-form.tsx:53 (`${VITE_BACKEND_API_URL}/auth/github`) — a user who has a `wafflebase login` waiting on the consent page and then clicks Sign in in another tab (or simply double-clicks/reloads the login link) clobbers the cookie, so the earlier callback is refused: `400 CLI login state expired` for the CLI, or `/login?error=login_state` for the browser. Before this change concurrent/retried starts were harmless because no cookie existed. A per-login cookie name (or a small set) would remove the collision.

verdict.reason: The premise — that both login flows write the same `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie — is false in this repository. The CLI branch issues a distinct cookie: github-auth.guard.ts:31 defines `CLI_STATE_COOKIE = 'wafflebase_cli_state'` (with a comment stating it is deliberately not `OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE` for precisely this collision scenario), and github-auth.guard.ts:294 calls `issueLoginCookie(context, CLI_STATE_COOKIE)`. Only the browser branch uses `OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE` (github-auth.guard.ts:302). The reviewer's cited lines 241 and 250 are `const mode = req.query?.mode` and a comment, containing no `issueLoginCookie` call. The consumer matches the split: auth.controller.ts:276 reads `OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE` only for `w.`-prefixed browser state, auth.controller.ts:294 reads `CLI_STATE_COOKIE` for CLI state, and `takeStateCookie` (auth.controller.ts:325-330) clears only the one named cookie, so one flow cannot spend the other's. Tests assert this (github-auth.guard.spec.ts:224-225; auth.controller.spec.ts:446-462 has a browser holding both cookies simultaneously). Therefore the described entry point (frontend sign-in link at login-form.tsx:53 clicked while a CLI consent page waits) does not clobber the CLI binding. The only residual is two concurrent *browser* starts overwriting the single browser cookie — a different, single-flow issue already covered elsewhere, conventional for state-cookie OAuth, and not a cross-consumer blast-radius breakage.
